newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Palestinians keep talking at cross purposes.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians keep talking at cross purposes.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians are still talking at cross purposes despite the best efforts of U.S. envoy Dennis Ross to save peacemaking after July's twin suicide bombings by Islamic militants.
Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials held another round of talks on Monday, the second day of Ross's mission.
Ross hailed the two meetings so far as steps towards reviving security cooperation between the Israelis and Palestinians.
His main task is to prepare for a trip to the region by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright which is expected to take place at the end of the month provided progress is made on security.
It will fall to Albright to try to revive substantive peace negotiations, which have been in limbo since Israel launched a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
While the security men seemed on track on Monday, Israeli and Palestinian politicians talked at cross purposes.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters after Ross met Arafat late on Monday night:

"We demand linking the security efforts to progress on the political issues so that we can resolve the crisis. Any progress on the security level without equal progress on the political track will be insufficient."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told MSNBC television: "We are looking for results. They have to fight terrorism. Period."
Ross tried to bring the two sides together on common ground.

"Security is something that serves Israeli interests and Palestinian interests. You have a common threat and you have a common enemy and it's important to deal with that as partners," Ross told reporters.
He added later: "There has to be a basis of security to be able to underpin and move the peace process and there has to be a political dimension ultimately for the peace process to succeed."

Netanyahu suspended resumption of substantive peace negotiations and sealed off the two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the July 30 suicide bombings at an Israeli market in which 16 people, including the attackers, were killed. He also stopped financial transfers to the Palestinian Authority.
He has vowed not to lift the sanctions until Arafat cracks down on militants.

Asked about the Israeli sanctions after his meeting with Arafat, Ross said: "Some measures that don't relate so clearly to security are measures that are not helpful and would be counter-productive." He did not elaborate.

"Political" matters for Palestinians are issues like the closing off of the West Bank and Gaza Strip and the Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem. They want the building stopped. Netanyahu has refused.
Arafat says he has fought militants though he stopped security cooperation with Israel over the settlement.
In Gaza City on Monday, thousands of Palestinian protesters marched down the main street demanding Israel free their imprisoned sons and end the closure.
Just outside Ramallah about 50 youths burned tyres and tried to throw stones at Israeli soldiers. Palestinian police entered Israeli-controlled territory to disperse the protesters.
In Amman, the Islamic militant group Hamas's spokesman Ibrahim Ghoshe warned Arafat against a crackdown, saying it would pit Palestinian against Palestinian.

Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, an Arafat aide, said in a statement the Palestinian Authority "will not allow Ghoshe or the likes of him to play with the fate of our people or harm the Authority or threaten it with terrorism or civil war".
Netanyahu has said Israel has had indications Hamas carried out the attack, even though Israeli and Palestinian officials have questioned the authenticity of a Hamas claim of responsibility.
Asked by reporters if pushing Arafat to crack down on militants might cause the Palestinian leader difficulties, Netanyahu said:
"Politically difficult things are all over the place. It's politically difficult for me to have my citizens blown up in the middle of our cities..."
In Washington on Monday, a U.S. State Department spokesman said Ross's mission would last another day or two. Ross is expected to meet Arafat and Netanyahu separately on Tuesday.
